title: Clarence Williams' publishing office and the Iroquois Theater
summary: As a boy he hung around Clarence Williams' office, swept up, and sang along to promote songs for a nickel; he loved the Iroquois on Sundays.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: I know Claris Williams, he had his music publishing company, well I guess it was a publishing company then, right around the corner on Tulane. Yeah. And I used to go around there and just hang around to hear the music and what not that was coming out. He would be playing, or different fathers would be in there playing and getting a thing. Well that was right around the corner on Tulane. Yeah.
I think 1100 and something is the address. I have some of the old sheet music published by P. Ronan. Is that right? Claris Williams, like Sister Kate and all that.

I remember that from a kid. And so I got, I was so interested in music at that time, I would always be hanging around out front to hear the sounds that were coming out. So he used to give me different little things to come on in and sweep the floor or something. And the Iroquois Theater on Ramport Street at that time, that was, that was the height. If I could get to the Iroquois on Sundays, that was it. You know, I would do anything to get some money to go to the Iroquois. And they had movies? They had movies, good westerns, and on Sundays they used to have live shows. Yeah. And one thing that stands out in my mind that when he wrote, My Mama's Baby Boy. My Mama's Baby Boy, one of those kind of things. And he would give us something, he would give all the kids that he knew, well here's a nickel now, when we come on you sing. He was promoting, from what I can recollect of it now, he was promoting songs, you know what I mean. And we would get in there and he would play it over and then we would join in on the course and start singing. My Mama's Baby Boy. Yeah. Used to whistle.
